bigIdea: Why do we celebrate harvests and give thanks?
readingSkill: Understanding the Setting (identifying time and place, and how setting affects characters)
contentArea: Social Studies & Science Fiction (Cultural Harvest Traditions and Space Agriculture)
selFocus: Self-Awareness & Thankfulness (recognizing what we appreciate in family, community, and daily life)
phonicsFocus: Final consonant blend -st (fast, last, lost, best, test, harvest, first)
grammarOrLanguageFocus: Expressing gratitude ('thankful for [noun]'), descriptive 'There is / There are', and reasons with 'Why / Because'

reading1.title: Chuseok: Korea's Harvest Festival
reading1.summary: Long ago in Korea, two teams had a month-long weaving contest to make cloth. On the full moon night, the king chose the winning team and gave a huge feast for both teams, starting Chuseok. Today, Chuseok remains an important three-day holiday at the end of summer. Families travel home to spend time together and celebrate the harvest. People eat special half-moon rice cakes called songpyeon, wear new clothes, and dance in circles. Families also hold a memorial ceremony where they bow and offer harvest food to honor their ancestors.
keySentences: Who can weave the most cloth? Two teams have a contest to find out.
Today, the festival of Chuseok is still an important holiday in Korea.
Chuseok is also a time for Koreans to remember their ancestors.

reading2.title: First Harvest
reading2.summary: A family works hard on an indoor farm, digging up vegetables and picking colorful fruit. The father worries because water is limited, but their crops grow into pink potatoes, purple corn, and orange peas. Mom suggests making an apple pie and inviting everyone to celebrate their very first harvest feast. The children, Ruth and August, ask if they can go outside to play first. Mom tells them to check their space suits and make sure they have plenty of air. The surprise setting is revealed to be a farming base on Mars!
keySentences: Harvest time is here. The family works hard on the farm.
“I know, let's get everyone together. We can have a feast!” says Ruth.
“Check your space suits before you go,” Mom says. “And make sure you have a lot of air.”

pageByPage.whatIsOnIt: Think Together. Activity A: Compare and contrast chart (What's the Same? / What's Different?). Activity B: Farmer role-play. My Reading Journal: continue the story.
pageByPage.instructionsAsWritten: A Think and write. Compare and contrast the two harvest stories in this unit. B Think and discuss. Imagine you are a farmer. Make a table about your harvest and your celebration. My Reading Journal: Be the author. Choose Chuseok or First Harvest. Read the ending again. Write and draw what happens next.
pageByPage.answersIfDeterminable: A Same: both have families, celebrate harvest, have big feasts, give thanks. Different: Chuseok is in Korea (Earth); First Harvest is on Mars (science fiction).

comprehensionQuestions.question: What was the prize for the winning team in the ancient weaving contest?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: A big feast for both teams given by the king.

comprehensionQuestions.question: What are two things Korean families are thankful for during Chuseok?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: The food from the harvest and their family / ancestors.

comprehensionQuestions.question: Why do you think families travel to their hometowns for Chuseok?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: They want to celebrate together, share food, and honor their ancestors.

comprehensionQuestions.question: Where does the family grow their food in 'First Harvest'?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: On the farm inside a greenhouse dome on Mars.

comprehensionQuestions.question: What special clothing do Ruth and August need before going outside?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: They need their space suits (with helmets and air).

comprehensionQuestions.question: Why was Dad worried at the beginning of 'First Harvest'?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: It is hard for plants to grow there because there isn't much water.

comprehensionQuestions.question: How are Chuseok and the harvest celebration on Mars similar?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: Both celebrations bring families together to enjoy a feast and give thanks for their hard work and food.

cultureOrContentFacts: Chuseok is Korea's traditional mid-autumn harvest festival, celebrated on the 15th day of the 8th lunar month under the full moon.
Songpyeon are traditional rice cakes shaped like half-moons and filled with sweet sesame seeds, honey, or beans.
Ganggangsullae is an ancient Korean circle dance performed by women holding hands under the harvest moon.
Charye is a traditional memorial service where families set a table with fresh harvest foods and bow to thank ancestors.
Growing food on Mars requires pressurized greenhouses, artificial heating, recycled water, and soil enrichment because Mars is cold and dry.

pictureNotes.describe: Illustrated hands presenting symbols of gratitude: video game controller, soccer ball, glowing sun, house, and assorted wrapped candies.
Photograph of a smiling mother, father, and young daughter dressed in vibrant hanbok behind a table of fresh harvest fruits and grains.
Two groups of women in traditional hanbok weaving cloth on wooden looms, and an ancient king arriving in red imperial robes.
Close-up photo of colorful green, white, and pink songpyeon, and a wide photo of dozens of women dancing Ganggangsullae in a giant circle.
Photograph of a man in traditional white coat and black hat arranging fruit, fish, and dishes on an ancestral charye table.
Father and daughter in futuristic blue and pink jumpsuits examining harvested purple carrots inside a geodesic transparent greenhouse dome.
Kitchen scene showing an oxygen meter on the wall marked 'O2' and a circular portal window looking out onto Martian domes.
Children putting on white and pink space helmets labeled 'MARS 3000' with reflections of the red planet's cratered surface.

difficultyFlags: ancestors: Concept can be abstract for A1; explain simply as 'grandparents of our grandparents' with family tree visuals.
weave / cloth: Distinguish noun (cloth) from verb (weave); demonstrate with interlaced fingers.
setting: Students may focus only on place; remind them that setting includes both time (past, future, season) and place (Korea, Mars).
science fiction twist: Some young learners might miss that Ruth and August are on Mars until page 37; scaffold with dome and space helmet clues.
